answer.label: Not Lenin — a Cold War attribution with no source
answer.authorDates: Credited to Vladimir Lenin (1870–1924), Russian revolutionary and first head of the Soviet state
answer.sourceLine: The sentence appears nowhere in Lenin’s collected writings, and Wikiquote files it under Misattributed. The earliest strong match Quote Investigator has located is a freestanding filler item in The Commonwealth of 31 October 1955 — thirty-one years after Lenin’s death — which credits him with a differently worded version on the sole authority of Major George Racey Jordan, an American anti-communist campaigner, and gives no work, date or occasion.

source.heading: The trail stops in 1955, not in Lenin

Not found. The nearest genuine text is “Left-Wing” Communism: an Infantile Disorder, written April–May 1920 and issued as a pamphlet that June, whose rope image is about British politicians rather than capitalists

source.excerpt: Lenin wrote, “When it comes time to hang the capitalists, they will vie with each other for the rope contract.” —Major George Racey Jordan
trail: June 1920 — Lenin publishes “Left-Wing” Communism: an Infantile Disorder, in which he says he wants to support the Labour politician Henderson “in the same way as the rope supports a hanged man”. The rope stands for a tactical vote in a British election, and nobody sells anything (Marxists Internet Archive ↗).

26 March 1924 — two months after Lenin’s death, Lord Emmott tells the House of Lords that Grigory Zinoviev had said the Bolsheviks should support the British Labour Party “as the rope ‘supports’ the man who hangs himself” — the same image, from a different Bolshevik (Quote Investigator ↗).

31 October 1955 — the earliest strong match Quote Investigator has located: a filler line in The Commonwealth crediting Lenin with “When it comes time to hang the capitalists, they will vie with each other for the rope contract”, sourced only to Major George Racey Jordan (Quote Investigator ↗).

30 June 1975 — Aleksandr Solzhenitsyn, speaking in Washington, tells it as an anecdote: Lenin promising “we will give a rope to the bourgeoisie and the bourgeoisie will hang itself with this rope”, and Karl Radek asking where they will get enough rope. QI notes it does not know how Solzhenitsyn acquired the story (Quote Investigator ↗).
source.excerptNote: That is the whole of it: a freestanding filler item in The Commonwealth of 31 October 1955, verified from scans by Quote Investigator. It is not the modern wording, it names no work, date or occasion, and it appeared thirty-one years after Lenin’s death in January 1924.

source.rightsNote: The famous wording has no identified author, no original work and no first-publication date, so no copyright status can honestly be asserted for it. The nearest genuine Lenin text — “Left-Wing” Communism: an Infantile Disorder, written April–May 1920 and issued as a pamphlet that June — is long out of copyright in its Russian original, but the standard English wording of that passage comes from Julius Katzer’s translation in the 1964 Progress Publishers Collected Works, a modern rendering whose own status is separate.

author.name: Vladimir Lenin
author.heading: Why it gets pinned on Lenin
author.metaLine: 1870–1924 · Russian revolutionary, first head of the Soviet state
author.bio: Vladimir Lenin led the Bolshevik seizure of power in 1917 and headed Soviet Russia until his death in January 1924, and he attracts manufactured quotations more reliably than almost any modern figure — a cynical line about capitalist greed sounds like him, and few English readers can check fifty-five volumes of Russian to find out. He did write a rope metaphor: in “Left-Wing” Communism: an Infantile Disorder (1920) he says he wants to back the British Labour politician Henderson “in the same way as the rope supports a hanged man” — but that is about a tactical vote in a British election, and nobody in it sells anything. Nothing resembling the rope-selling sentence has been found in his published work.

misattribution.heading: A Cold War quotation in search of an author
misattribution.intro: Three versions circulate — ‘the capitalists will sell us the rope with which we will hang them’, ‘when it comes time to hang the capitalists, they will sell us the rope’, and ‘the last capitalist we hang shall be the one who sold us the rope’ — pinned variously on Lenin, Stalin and Marx. None of the three has ever been traced to any of them.

items.why: Wikiquote ↗ files this exact sentence under Misattributed, citing They Never Said It (p. 64) for the finding that there is no evidence Lenin said it, and suggests it may derive as a confused paraphrase of a genuine 1920 passage in which the rope supports a hanged man and no one sells anything.

Jordan was a US Army Air Corps Lend-Lease control officer who became a public anti-communist after testifying to Congress in 1949 (Wikipedia ↗). The filler item carrying his name in The Commonwealth of 31 October 1955 names no work, date or occasion for the alleged remark (Quote Investigator ↗).

Senator Barry Goldwater’s 1979 memoir With No Apologies gave the line to Stalin, hedged as something he said ‘to this effect’. Quote Investigator finds no substantive evidence for the Stalin attribution (Quote Investigator ↗).

A fund manager testifying before a US Senate committee in 2007 attributed ‘the last capitalist we hang shall be the one who sold us the rope’ to Marx and Lenin together. QI finds no substantive evidence for Marx either (Quote Investigator ↗).

misattribution.truthLine: Best available verdict: a Cold War coinage with no author. The Austrian quotation researcher Gerald Krieghofer finds no digitised text in German, English or Russian before 1950 in which the line appears as a Lenin quote, and calls it an invention of the Cold War era (Zitatforschung ↗), while Quote Investigator calls the evidence linking the saying to Lenin weak because the first citation appeared in 1955, many years after his death in 1924 (Quote Investigator ↗).

context.heading: How a slogan outran its source
lead: The line earned its fame as an argument, not as a quotation. From the late 1950s it was deployed in American debates over trade with the Soviet bloc: if Lenin himself had predicted that capitalists would sell the Communists the means of their own destruction, every export licence became evidence for the prosecution. Quote Investigator records it in a syndicated Victor Riesel column on 12 January 1959, in a congressional hearing on 29 January 1959 where Representative Walter H. Judd ascribed it to Lenin, and in a letter to Aviation Week and Space Technology that May.

What keeps it alive is that the underlying thought is not absurd. A passage attributed to Lenin by the memoirist I. U. Annenkov, printed in the émigré journal Novyi Zhurnal in September 1961 and later logged by the Congressional Research Service, has capitalists furnishing credits and equipment and thereby working “on the preparation of their own suicide”. That is the same idea — but it reached print thirty-seven years after Lenin died, in a wording whose only warrant is Annenkov’s own account of examining Lenin’s manuscripts in 1924, and it contains no rope.
detailsBody: Long before any Bolshevik, English had ‘give a man enough rope and he will hang himself’ — a proverb of the mid-17th century in which nobody sells the rope. Quote Investigator traces socialist uses of the image through Samuel E. Keeble’s Industrial Day-Dreams (1896), which argued that capitalism, ‘by giving it rope enough’, would hang itself, and through the 1901 proceedings of the Socialist Labor Party’s tenth national convention, where delegate Thomas Curran spoke of weaving ‘a rope with which we will hang the capitalist class’.

The closest pre-1955 match is not about Lenin at all. A profile of the Soviet diplomat Maxim Litvinov by S. Dmitrijewski in the Review of Reviews of July 1931 described millionaires financing a Bolshevik newspaper in 1905 and thereby helping to ‘weave the rope from which many of them should hang later on’ — the meaning of the saying, decades before anyone put it in Lenin’s mouth.
context.pull: The trail runs backwards through Cold War pamphleteering, not forwards from anything Lenin wrote.

sourcesVerified.claim: Quote Investigator's earliest strong match is a filler item in The Commonwealth: Official Journal of the Commonwealth Club of California, 31 October 1955, vol. 31 no. 44, p. 268, reading 'Lenin wrote, "When it comes time to hang the capitalists, they will vie with each other for the rope contract." —Major George Racey Jordan', with no documentary source specified.

QI concludes the evidence linking the saying to Lenin is weak because the first citation appeared in 1955, many years after Lenin's death in 1924, and that there is no substantive evidence supporting the attributions to Joseph Stalin or Karl Marx.

QI records the 1896 Keeble 'giving it rope enough it will hang itself' passage, the 1901 Socialist Labor Party convention remark by delegate Thomas Curran about weaving 'a rope with which we will hang the capitalist class', Lord Emmott's 26 March 1924 Hansard report of Zinoviev's 'as the rope supports the man who hangs himself', and the July 1931 Review of Reviews profile by S. Dmitrijewski about millionaires helping 'weave the rope from which many of them should hang later on'.

QI records Victor Riesel's syndicated column of 12 January 1959, Representative Walter H. Judd's 29 January 1959 remark in a House Foreign Affairs briefing, a May 1959 Aviation Week and Space Technology letter, Solzhenitsyn's 30 June 1975 Washington speech anecdote featuring Karl Radek, Barry Goldwater's 1979 memoir With No Apologies attributing it to Stalin 'to this effect', and a 2007 US Senate committee witness attributing it to Marx and Lenin.

QI cites Respectfully Quoted (Congressional Research Service, 1989) for a thematically related passage attributed to Lenin by I. U. Annenkov in 'Remembrances of Lenin', Novyi Zhurnal / New Review, September 1961, p. 147, in which capitalists supplying credits and equipment 'will work on the preparation of their own suicide'.

Wikiquote lists 'We will hang the capitalists with the rope that they sell us.' in its Misattributed section for Vladimir Lenin, citing They Never Said It p. 64 for there being no evidence Lenin said it, and suggests it may derive as a confused paraphrase from '"Left-Wing" Communism: an Infantile Disorder' (1920).

Lenin's genuine text reads: 'with my vote, I want to support Henderson in the same way as the rope supports a hanged man', in the section '"Left-Wing" Communism in Great Britain' of "Left-Wing" Communism: an Infantile Disorder.

"Left-Wing" Communism: an Infantile Disorder was written April–May 1920 and first published as a pamphlet in June 1920; the marxists.org English text is Julius Katzer's translation from Collected Works vol. 31 (Progress Publishers, USSR, 1964), and '"Left-Wing" Communism in Great Britain' is its ninth section.

Gerald Krieghofer's Zitatforschung finds the quotation in no digitised German, English or Russian text as a Lenin quote before 1950, traces its evolution from a 1958 English anecdote, and concludes with They Never Said It and Wikiquote that it is a Cold War-era invention (a 'Kuckuckszitat').

George Racey Jordan (4 January 1898 – 5 May 1966) was an American military officer who served as a Lend-Lease control officer in the US Army Air Corps and gained nationwide attention in December 1949 by testifying to Congress about wartime deliveries to the Soviet Union.
Vladimir Lenin was born 22 April 1870 and died 21 January 1924; he was a Russian revolutionary and the first head of government of Soviet Russia from 1917 to 1924.
